methods: reducing higher powers using the equation
statement: Let $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+1$. (i) Show that if $\alpha$ is a root of $f(x)=0$ then $\alpha^{2}-2$ is also a root. (ii) Deduce that the three roots of $f(x)=0$ may be written as $\alpha,\ \alpha^{2}-2,\ \alpha^{4}-4\alpha^{2}+2$ where $\alpha$ is any one root, and explain why they are distinct.
solution: (i) If $f(\alpha)=0$ then $\alpha^{3}=3\alpha-1$. Substitute $x=\alpha^{2}-2$: expand $(\alpha^{2}-2)^{3}=\alpha^{6}-6\alpha^{4}+12\alpha^{2}-8$. Reduce powers using $\alpha^{3}=3\alpha-1$: $\alpha^{4}=3\alpha^{2}-\alpha$ and $\alpha^{6}=(3\alpha-1)^{2}=9\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+1$. Then $x^{3}-3x+1=(9\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+1)-6(3\alpha^{2}-\alpha)+12\alpha^{2}-8-3(\alpha^{2}-2)+6+1$; the $\alpha^{2}$, $\alpha$ and constant terms all cancel, giving $0$. So $\alpha^{2}-2$ is a root. (ii) Repeating gives a third root $(\alpha^{2}-2)^{2}-2=\alpha^{4}-4\alpha^{2}+2$. Distinctness: if $\alpha=\alpha^{2}-2$ then $\alpha=2$ or $-1$, but $f(2)=f(-1)=3\neq0$; similarly no two of the three coincide. Hence three distinct roots.
hints: Use alpha^3=3alpha-1 to reduce every higher power to a linear term.
